Skye: Where Motorcycling Meets Magic

The Isle of Skye is the jewel of Scotland's west coast and one of the most extraordinary motorcycle destinations in Europe. Its jagged Cuillin ridge, otherworldly rock formations, and constantly changing light create a landscape that feels more like Iceland than Britain. The roads are varied, the scenery is beyond superlatives, and the sense of being somewhere truly special never fades.

Getting There

Skye is connected to the mainland by the Skye Bridge at Kyle of Lochalsh — toll-free and open year-round. The alternative is the Glenelg-Kylerhea ferry, a tiny vessel that carries just six cars. The ferry is seasonal (Easter-October) but the crossing, through waters where otters and seals are common, is worth the detour.

The Best Roads on Skye

Skye's roads are predominantly single-track with passing places in the north and west, with wider A-roads in the south. Key rides include:

  • A87 Skye Bridge to Portree — The main road, flowing bends with Cuillin views
  • B8083 to Elgol — Dead-end road with the finest view in Scotland: the Cuillins across Loch Scavaig
  • A855 Trotternish Loop — Circular route around the peninsula, passing the Old Man of Storr and Quiraing
  • B8009 to Neist Point — Westernmost point with lighthouse and dramatic cliff views

Must-See Stops

The Quiraing in the Trotternish Peninsula is Skye's most photographed landscape — a surreal landslip of pinnacles, plateaux, and hidden valleys. The Old Man of Storr is the iconic rocky pinnacle visible from the A855. The Fairy Pools at Glen Brittle are crystal-clear waterfalls flowing from the Cuillins — magical in any weather.

Skye in good weather is spectacular. Skye in bad weather is atmospheric and dramatic. There is no bad time to visit Skye — only different moods.

Weather and When to Visit

Skye's weather is notoriously changeable. Rain is common year-round, and the island can be shrouded in cloud one moment and bathed in golden light the next. May-June offers the longest days and (usually) the driest weather. July-August brings midges — carry repellent. September-October brings autumn colours and often settled weather.

Accommodation and Facilities

Portree is Skye's main town with hotels, restaurants, and fuel. Broadford in the south has a fuel station and supermarket. Beyond these, facilities are limited — book accommodation well in advance, especially in summer. Wild camping is permitted under Scottish right to roam laws. The Three Chimneys restaurant near Dunvegan is world-class if you fancy a splurge.

Practical Tips for Motorcyclists

Skye's single-track roads require patience and courtesy. Pull into passing places on your left and never park in them. Sheep wander freely on the roads, especially in spring. Fuel is available in Portree, Broadford, and Armadale — don't leave it to chance elsewhere. The island is busy with campervans and tour buses in summer — early morning riding (before 9am) is the secret to enjoying the roads in peace. faq.q: How do I get to the Isle of Skye by motorcycle?
faq.a: The simplest route is the toll-free Skye Bridge at Kyle of Lochalsh, open year-round. For something more memorable, take the seasonal Glenelg-Kylerhea ferry, a tiny vessel carrying just six cars that runs from Easter to October. The crossing passes through waters where otters and seals are common, and it makes a worthwhile detour.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Skye?
faq.a: May and June bring the longest days and usually the driest weather, making them ideal for riding. July and August are warm but midges can be fierce, so carry repellent. September and October deliver autumn colours and often settled conditions. Skye's weather is changeable year-round, so pack waterproofs whatever the season.

faq.q: Where can I get fuel on Skye?
faq.a: Fuel is available in Portree, Broadford and Armadale. Beyond these three points the island has no reliable fuel, so fill up before heading to remote spots like Elgol or Neist Point. Never leave fuel to chance on the single-track dead-end roads.

faq.q: Where should I stay and eat on Skye?
faq.a: Portree is the main hub with hotels, restaurants and services, while Broadford in the south is quieter with a supermarket. Wild camping is permitted under Scottish right-to-roam laws. For a splurge, the Three Chimneys restaurant near Dunvegan is world-class.

faq.q: Are Skye's roads difficult to ride?
faq.a: Skye's northern and western roads are predominantly single-track with passing places, while the south has wider A-roads such as the A87 from the bridge to Portree. Pull into passing places on your left, never park in them, and watch for sheep wandering onto the road, especially in spring.
